## Numbers 35 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1 — Setting
The chapter opens with the familiar formula placing Israel “on the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho.” Both **Pulpit** and **Gill** note this is the same setting as Numbers 33:50 and 36:13 — the final legislative section before the conquest. God now provides for the Levites, who had no tribal inheritance.
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/35.htm
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/35.htm

---

### v. 2 — Cities for the Levites
The tribes must give the Levites cities and surrounding pasturelands from their own inheritance. **Pulpit** explains that although the Levites were already endowed with tithes and offerings (Num 18:21), they still needed homes and land for cattle. The Mosaic ideal was not a celibate, detached clergy; Levites were to enjoy ordinary family life. **Ellicott** says the Levites’ dispersion was primarily for instructing the tribes in God’s law (Deut 33:10). **Gill** calls it “reasonable and requisite” that ministers of God have habitations. **Enduring Word** (Guzik) points out this did not contradict Num 18:20 (“I am your portion”) because the total area assigned was only about 15 square miles (0.1% of Canaan).
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/35.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/35.htm
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/35.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-35/

---

### v. 3 — Purposes of the Pasturelands
The cities were for dwelling; the “suburbs” (Hebrew *migrash*, “pasture” or “paddock”) were for cattle, goods, and all livestock. **Pulpit** explains that “cattle” (*behemah*) means oxen, camels, and draught animals; “goods” (*rekush*) means sheep and goats. **Ellicott** concurs: *migrash* denotes pasture ground into which flocks are driven.
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/35.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/35.htm

---

### vv. 4–5 — Dimensions of the Pasturelands
The measurements are 1,000 cubits from the wall outward (v.4), then 2,000 cubits on each side (v.5). These verses are notoriously difficult.

**Jewish tradition** (cited by Gill, Jarchi) held that the inner 1,000 cubits were for cattle/goods, and the outer 2,000 for fields and vineyards — making a total band 3,000 cubits wide. **Pulpit** reviews three theories: (a) 1,000 for pasture plus 2,000 for fields/vineyards; (b) the 2,000 cubits equals city-wall length plus 1,000 on each side (Michaelis); (c) an approximate measurement with 1,000 cubit depth × 2,000 cubit width on each side. Pulpit finds all three problematic but leans toward (c) as simplest.

**Ellicott** notes the Greek LXX reads “2,000” in both v.4 and v.5, adding to the difficulty. He describes the Jewish view (1,000 for cattle, 2,000 for vineyards) and Michaelis’s alternative. **Guzik** (Enduring Word) mentions that later Judaism based the “Sabbath day’s journey” (2,000 cubits) on this passage.
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/35.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/35.htm
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/35.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-35/

---

### v. 6 — Six Cities of Refuge, Plus Forty-Two
Among the Levitical cities, six were designated “cities of refuge” for the manslayer. **Gill** adds that Jewish tradition held *all* 48 Levitical cities provided some asylum, but the six were specially set apart: their gates received the fugitive whether he knew they were refuge cities or not, while the other 42 only received him if he came knowingly.

**Ellicott** explains the main reasons refuge cities were Levitical: (1) they were consecrated to the Lord (Josh 20:7, Hebrew “consecrated”); (2) priests and Levites were the natural administrators of justice.
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/35.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/35.htm

---

### vv. 7–8 — Forty-Eight Cities Distributed Proportionally
The 48 cities total (about 1,000 Levites per city, given ~50,000 Levites per Num 26:62). **Pulpit** notes the 48 may be symbolic (12 × 4, both numbers of universality) or simply practical. Larger tribes gave more cities; smaller tribes gave fewer. However, **Pulpit** observes the rule wasn't perfectly executed: Judah-Simeon gave nine, most gave four, and Naphtali gave three (Josh 21).

**Enduring Word** (Guzik) stresses the missional purpose: the Levites were “sprinkled” throughout Israel as teachers of God’s word, like salt preserving meat. No Israelite would be far from biblical instruction. This, Guzik argues, is God’s model for the church — Christians distributed throughout society rather than cloistered together.
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/35.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-35/

---

### vv. 9–12 — Purpose of the Cities of Refuge
The Lord now gives the purpose: when Israel crosses the Jordan, they must designate cities where a person who kills “unintentionally” (*bisgaga*, the same word as “unintentional” sins in Num 15:22–29) may flee from the “avenger of blood” (*goel*). The avenger (kinsman-redeemer) had the cultural duty to avenge family blood. **Pulpit** gives a lengthy analysis: the *goel* was the “protector of family rights” — redeeming property, avenging blood. God both sanctioned and regulated this ancient custom.

**Enduring Word** (Guzik) notes that the avenger’s role was never directly *commanded* by Scripture; it was a broad cultural practice that Scripture *regulated*. Genesis 9:6 provided the theological basis.

**Benson’s Commentary** (early Methodist) explains the avenger was the nearest kinsman, to whom belonged “the right of redemption of the lands of, and vindication of the injury done to, the person deceased.”
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/35.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-35/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/numbers-35.html

---

### vv. 13–14 — Placement: Three East, Three West
Six cities total: three east of Jordan, three in Canaan proper. **Ellicott** says Moses himself appointed the eastern three (Bezer, Ramoth-Gilead, Golan — Deut 4:43), but the western three were appointed only after the conquest under Joshua (Kedesh, Shechem, Hebron — Josh 20:7). **Gill** notes the Jewish teaching that none functioned as a refuge until all six were established.

**Pulpit** notes a fascinating detail: Deuteronomy 19:8–9 appears to command *three additional* cities if Israel’s territory was enlarged — which the rabbis expected to be fulfilled in the Messianic age. Gill adds this rabbinic expectation, commenting wryly that “the Messiah is come already, and is the antitype of them all.”
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/35.htm
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/35.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/35.htm

---

### v. 15 — Open to Israelite, Stranger, and Sojourner
Protection extended equally to native Israelites, the *ger* (foreigner with temporary residence), and the *toshab* (settled sojourner). **Ellicott** explains the distinction between these terms. **Gill** notes that rabbinic teaching restricted the sojourner’s privilege (only if he killed another sojourner), but Gill rejects this as having “no foundation in the text.”

**Gill** (quoting himself in a rare direct theological application) says: “Christ is for all sinners, even the chief of sinners — Jews or Gentiles; they are all one in Christ.”
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/35.htm
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/35.htm

---

### vv. 16–18 — Murder by Instrument of Iron, Stone, or Wood
These three verses establish that if the killer used an instrument *likely to cause death*, he is a murderer regardless of claimed intent. The categories are: iron implement (v.16), a stone “of the hand” (i.e., large enough to fill the hand, sufficient to kill — v.17), or a wooden hand-weapon (club — v.18). **Gill** explains the logic: the *choice of weapon* demonstrates intent; no one strikes another with a deadly instrument without murderous design. **Pulpit** adds that iron was specifically named even though bronze weapons were more common, because where iron appears, it is always associated with war.
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/35.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/35.htm

---

### v. 19 — The Avenger Shall Put the Murderer to Death
The *goel* (avenger of blood) himself acts as executioner. **Gill** cites Onkelos’s Targum that this was to be done “when he is condemned by judgment” — i.e., not vigilante justice but judicial execution. **Enduring Word** likewise emphasises that the avenger’s right was not unrestrained; Scripture reserves vengeance to God (Deut 32:35; Rom 12:19).
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/35.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-35/

---

### vv. 20–21 — Murder by Malice: Pushing, Hurling, or Striking in Enmity
These verses address murder discerned by *motive* rather than weapon: pushing out of hatred, lying in wait and hurling something, or striking with the fist in enmity. The key diagnostic is premeditation and hostile intent. **Pulpit** observes the law here considers not merely sudden anger versus malice aforethought, but a deliberate fatal blow. **Ellicott** renders these verses in the past tense (“if he thrust him… if he smote him…”), treating them as case law describing what has already happened.
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/35.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/35.htm

---

### vv. 22–24 — Manslaughter: Sudden, Without Enmity, Accidental
These verses describe the contrasting scenarios: pushing suddenly without enmity, throwing something without lying in wait, or dropping a stone without seeing the victim — all cases of true accident. **Pulpit** notes the example in Deut 19:5 (an axe-head flying off while chopping wood). The “congregation” must then judge between slayer and avenger.

**Pulpit** makes an important observation about the word “congregation” (*edah*): it does *not* mean merely the local elders (as in Josh 20:4 for the preliminary hearing) but the whole assembly of Israel in its representative judicial capacity. The local elders gave temporary shelter pending full trial before the *edah*.

**Enduring Word**: Both sides of the story were heard; the city of refuge did not guarantee immunity — it guaranteed a fair trial.
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/35.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-35/

---

### v. 25 — The Manslayer Must Remain Until the High Priest’s Death
If declared innocent of murder, the congregation escorts him back to the city of refuge, where he must remain until the death of the high priest anointed with holy oil.

**Ellicott** explains the theological rationale: though the death was accidental, bloodshed still demanded expiation. The high priest’s death had a “symbolical or representative character,” typifying the death of Christ, “the great High Priest who… by His death made a propitiation for the sins of the world.”

**Pulpit** is more cautious: it is “not easy to see why the death of the high priest should have set the fugitive free… except as foreshadowing the death of Christ.” He suggests the high priest, as chief minister of God’s law, was effectively the *goel* of the whole nation — when he died, all blood-feuds lapsed because they had been commenced in his name.

**Gill** and **Benson** both make the Christological connection: Benson says the death of the high priest shows “that the death of Christ, the true High-Priest… is the only means whereby sins are pardoned, and sinners set at liberty.”

**Enduring Word** (Guzik): The only thing that could liberate the manslayer was the high priest’s death. This points to Jesus, but with a crucial difference — our High Priest *ever lives* (Heb 6:20; 7:16, 24), and His death atones not for the innocent but for the guilty.
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/35.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/35.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/numbers-35.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-35/

---

### vv. 26–28 — If the Manslayer Leaves the City
If the manslayer ventures outside the city limits, the avenger may kill him without guilt. The manslayer “should have remained” (*yashab* — to dwell, sit, remain). **Ellicott** draws a spiritual parallel: just as the Israelite’s bodily safety depended on staying inside the city, the believer’s spiritual safety depends on “exclusive reliance upon the merits and efficacy of the atoning death and righteousness of Christ” (Acts 4:12).

**Spurgeon** (quoted in Enduring Word) says: “He was therefore to suffer perpetual banishment, even for causing death accidentally, in order that it might be seen how much God regarded the rights of blood, and how fearful a thing it is to put a man to death in any way.”

**Enduring Word** notes that even the innocent manslayer’s life was profoundly disrupted — he had to leave his home, perhaps his family, and live in exile within the city. Tragedy touches even the innocent.
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/35.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-35/

---

### v. 29 — A Statute for Generations
This was not temporary legislation but a “statutory ordinance” (*chuqqat mishpat*) binding wherever Israel dwelt. **Gill** does not elaborate here separately, but the verse anchors the perpetuity of the principles involved.
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/35.htm

---

### v. 30 — Multiple Witnesses Required
No one could be executed on the testimony of a single witness. **Ellicott** notes that the specific number (“two or three”) is spelled out in Deut 17:6 and 19:15, but the principle is established here. **Benson** adds that Jewish tradition held that where there was only one witness, the accused was not released but imprisoned and fed “bread and water.”

**Enduring Word** highlights that the witnesses themselves were obligated to be the first to carry out the execution (Deut 17:7), ensuring sincerity and accountability — no one would testify lightly if they had to cast the first stone.
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/35.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/numbers-35.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-35/

---

### vv. 31–32 — No Ransom for Murder or for the Manslayer’s Early Release
No monetary payment (*kopher*, “ransom” or “satisfaction”) could substitute for a murderer’s execution. Nor could a manslayer buy his freedom from the city of refuge before the high priest’s death. **Ellicott** notes the contrast with other ancient Near Eastern practices where blood-money was accepted. **Pulpit** calls this “rigid severity” that impressed on the people the sanctity of human life.

**Wenham** (cited in Enduring Word): “Atonement for manslaughter came through the death of the high priest… Just as a murderer cannot buy his life for money, so a manslaughterer cannot purchase freedom. Both have caused the death of another man, and only the death of a man can atone for the killing.”
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/35.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/35.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-35/

---

### vv. 33–34 — Blood Pollutes the Land; The Lord Dwells Among Israel
Bloodshed defiles the land itself, and no atonement can be made for it “except by the blood of the one who shed it.” The reason: “I, the LORD, dwell among the Israelites.” **Pulpit** says this is the theological climax — the land must be kept clean because it is the Holy Land where God dwells. **Enduring Word** (Guzik) applies this soberly to modern nations where unpunished murders “pollute the land.”

**Constable** (DCC, via search results) explains: “The reason for this was that ‘blood pollutes the land’ (v.33). That is, these crimes brought uncleanness on the land because they involved killing people without divine authorization.”
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/35.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-35/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-35.html

---

## Tradition-Specific Emphases and Differences

### Reformed / Baptist (Spurgeon, Gill, Ligonier)

**Spurgeon** developed the cities of refuge as a full-scale type of Christ in his sermon “The Sinner’s Refuge” (Sermon 2621). He stresses that the city’s safety rested *not* on walls or bars but solely on *Divine appointment* — and so with Christ: “Divine appointment was the only thing which made the city of refuge secure.” However, Spurgeon emphasises a *contrast*: the city of refuge only helped the *innocent* (the accidental manslayer), but Christ welcomes the *guilty*. “Our Savior has come into the world to save not those who have, by mistake and error, committed sin, but those who have fearfully transgressed against well-known Divine Commandments.”
- https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons45/sermons45.xix.html

**Ligonier** (Reformed) highlights God’s promise-keeping fidelity: the Levitical cities promised in Numbers 35 were actually given in Joshua 21, demonstrating that “the Lord always does what He says He will do.”
- https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/our-promise-keeping-lord

**Gill** (Reformed Baptist) sees Christ as the antitype of all the cities of refuge and notes rabbinic expectation of three *additional* cities in the Messianic age, concluding that “the Messiah is come already, and is the antitype of them all.”
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/numbers/35.htm

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word — David Guzik)

Guzik emphasises the *missional* dispersal of the Levites as a model for the church: Christians are to be “sprinkled throughout the whole world, influencing people for Jesus Christ.” The typology of the cities of refuge is developed extensively, with the key *difference* that “the cities of refuge protected only the innocent from the avenger of blood, but Jesus’s refuge welcomes the guilty — a crucial distinction that highlights the gospel’s radical grace.” Guzik also applies vv.33–34 to modern nations, warning that unpunished murders defile a land.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-35/

### Methodist / Wesleyan (Benson’s Commentary)

**Benson** draws the Christological typology directly: the cities of refuge were assigned to the Levites “perhaps to signify that it is only in Christ (whom the Levitical priests represented) that sinners find refuge and safety from the destroyer.” On the high priest’s death, Benson says it shows “that the death of Christ, the true High-Priest, whom the others represented, is the only means whereby sins are pardoned, and sinners set at liberty.” Benson also notes that where there was only one witness, Jewish tradition held the accused was imprisoned — a “wise precaution to prevent the shedding of innocent blood.”
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/numbers-35.html

### Anglican (Ellicott)

**Ellicott** gives careful attention to the Hebrew terms and legal distinctions (e.g., *ger* vs. *toshab* in v.15; the construction of vv.6–8). His Christological reading centres on the high priest’s death as “a type of that of the great High Priest who, through the eternal Spirit, offered Himself without spot to God.” Ellicott also emphasises the *goel* as “redeemer” — the same word used of God as Redeemer in Job 19:25 — linking the avenger’s office to Christ’s redemptive work.
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/numbers/35.htm

### Lutheran

No distinctively Lutheran commentary on Numbers 35 was found among the searched sites (lcms.org, 1517.org), though the general typological reading of the cities of refuge as picturing Christ is shared broadly across Protestant traditions.

### Catholic and Orthodox

No results were retrieved from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org within the search limits. The Catholic and Orthodox readings of this passage were not accessible from the designated sites.

### Modern Scholarship

No results were retrieved from bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org within the search limits. However, **Wenham** (Gordon Wenham, cited in Enduring Word) represents modern evangelical scholarship: he notes the total Levitical area was about 0.1% of Canaan, and he argues that “atonement for manslaughter came through the death of the high priest” — a human death atoning for a human death, the principle being that “only the death of a man can atone for the killing.”
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-35/

### Summary of the Typological Consensus

Across **Spurgeon** (Baptist), **Benson** (Methodist), **Ellicott** (Anglican), **Gill** (Reformed Baptist), and **Guzik** (Pentecostal), there is strong agreement that the cities of refuge prefigure Christ as the sinner’s refuge. The points of the typology consistently noted are:

1. **Divine appointment** — safety rests on God’s word, not walls
2. **Accessibility** — roads were built, cities were evenly placed, open to all
3. **Priestly administration** — the cities were Levitical
4. **Liberation through the high priest’s death** — pointing to Christ’s atoning death
5. **The necessity of staying within** — abiding in Christ for safety (Heb 6:18)

The one point of *contrast* repeatedly emphasised (Spurgeon, Guzik): the earthly cities only sheltered the *innocent* (accidental manslayer), but Christ welcomes the *guilty* who flee to Him in faith.
